questions.stem: Which character delimits a search macro reference?

options.text: The backtick, as in `` `mymacro` ``
options.explanation: The backtick shares a key with the tilde. It is the only delimiter that triggers macro expansion.

options.text: The single quotation mark, as in 'mymacro'
options.explanation: Single quotes do not invoke a macro. The text is treated as an ordinary search term.

options.text: The double quotation mark, as in "mymacro"
options.explanation: Double quotes also fail to expand, and in fact macros inside quoted values are explicitly not expanded.

options.text: The dollar sign, as in $mymacro$
options.explanation: Dollar signs delimit argument tokens inside a macro definition, not the macro reference itself.

questions.overallExplanation: Backticks invoke, dollar signs substitute. Two different jobs and two different characters, and mixing them up is the most common macro error.

guide.blueprintTitle: Create and use a basic macro
guide.verdictNote: The platform does not expand macros inside quoted values, so a backtick reference buried in a quoted string will not fire either.

docs.title: Use search macros in searches (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Macro references are enclosed in backtick characters.

questions.stem: A macro takes three arguments. What must it be named in Settings, and how is it invoked?

options.text: Named `mymacro(3)`, invoked as `` `mymacro(a,b,c)` ``
options.explanation: The stored name carries the argument count. The invocation carries the actual values.

options.text: Named `mymacro`, invoked as `` `mymacro(3)` ``
options.explanation: This reverses the two. The number in the invocation would be read as a single argument value.

options.text: Named `mymacro(a,b,c)`, invoked as `` `mymacro(3)` ``
options.explanation: Argument names go in the separate Arguments field, not into the macro name.

options.text: Named `mymacro`, invoked as `` `mymacro(a,b,c)` ``
options.explanation: Calling with arguments when only a bare-name macro exists is an error rather than a call with arguments.

questions.overallExplanation: The documentation is explicit: if your search macro includes two arguments, name it mymacro(2). `[foobar]` and `[foobar(1)]` are different macros, not one macro with an optional argument.

guide.blueprintTitle: Add and use arguments with a macro
guide.verdictNote: Because the count is part of the name, you can define several macros sharing a base name with different arity, and they coexist independently.

docs.title: Define search macros in Settings (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Name a macro with its argument count, for example mymacro(2).

questions.stem: How are argument names written in the Arguments field, and how are they referenced in the Definition?

options.text: Bare and comma-delimited in Arguments, as `val, rate`; wrapped in dollar signs in the Definition, as `$val$`
options.explanation: Arguments takes a comma-delimited string of names. The Definition references them with the dollar-sign token pattern.

options.text: Dollar-wrapped in both places
options.explanation: Adding dollar signs in the Arguments field is a common error; that field wants bare names.

options.text: Bare in both places
options.explanation: Without dollar signs the Definition would treat the name as literal search text and never substitute.

options.text: Backtick-wrapped in the Definition
options.explanation: Backticks invoke other macros. They do not mark argument substitution.

questions.overallExplanation: Two quoting rules pull in opposite directions here. Macros are not expanded inside quoted values, but the $<arg>$ pattern is replaced globally, including inside quoted strings.

guide.blueprintTitle: Define arguments and variables for a macro
guide.verdictNote: Argument names may contain only alphanumeric characters, underscores and hyphens, with no repeats. The manual separately warns against hyphens in macro names.

docs.title: Define search macros in Settings (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Arguments is a comma-delimited string of argument names; the definition uses $arg$.

questions.stem: A macro has a validation expression, and a user supplies an argument that fails it. What does the user see?

options.text: The validation error message, with the search never dispatched.
options.explanation: Validation runs before dispatch, so the search does not execute at all and the configured error message is displayed.

options.text: Zero events, as though the search matched nothing.
options.explanation: An empty result set would be indistinguishable from a genuine no-match. Validation is designed to be louder than that.

options.text: The search runs with the argument replaced by a null value.
options.explanation: No substitution of a default happens. The search is stopped.

options.text: A warning in the job log, with the search running anyway.
options.explanation: Failing validation blocks execution rather than annotating it.

questions.overallExplanation: A Boolean validation expression succeeds on true and fails on false or NULL, with errormsg supplying the message. A non-Boolean validation expression inverts that: it succeeds on NULL and fails by returning the message itself.

guide.blueprintTitle: Define arguments and variables for a macro
guide.verdictNote: The two validation modes behaving oppositely is unusual enough to be examinable. Boolean: true is good. Non-Boolean: NULL is good.

docs.title: macros.conf spec (Admin Manual 10.4)
docs.note: validation and errormsg settings, and the Boolean versus non-Boolean behaviour.

questions.stem: Where does macro expansion sit in the sequence of search-time operations?

options.text: Nowhere in it; expansion is textual and happens before the search is parsed.
options.explanation: The nine-step sequence contains no macro step. A macro is replaced with its text before parsing begins.

options.text: Between field aliases and calculated fields.
options.explanation: That slot belongs to nothing; aliases at step 5 are followed directly by calculated fields at step 6.

options.text: Immediately after lookups.
options.explanation: Step 7 is followed by event types. Macros are not part of this ordering at all.

options.text: Last, after tags.
options.explanation: Tags are the final search-time operation, and macros are not a search-time knowledge object in this sense.

questions.overallExplanation: A macro is a text substitution performed on the search string. By the time the nine search-time operations run, the macro has already been replaced and is indistinguishable from typed SPL.

guide.verdictNote: This is why a macro can contain anything at all, including whole pipelines, while an event type definition cannot even contain a pipe.

docs.title: Search macros (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Macros are reusable search string fragments expanded into the search.

questions.stem: A macro should encapsulate `| tstats count WHERE index=web BY _time`. How should the definition be written?

options.text: Without the leading pipe, putting the pipe in front of the reference instead.
options.explanation: The definition holds `tstats count WHERE index=web BY _time` and the search reads `` | `mymacro` ``. The pipe lives at the call site.

options.text: With the leading pipe, so the macro is self-contained.
options.explanation: Keeping the pipe in the definition produces a doubled or misplaced pipe once the text is substituted.

options.text: With the leading pipe, and invoked without a preceding pipe.
options.explanation: This is the documented mistake. The convention is the reverse.

options.text: A generating command cannot be placed in a macro at all.
options.explanation: It can. Only the placement of the leading pipe needs care.

questions.overallExplanation: Because expansion is textual, the surrounding pipe structure is your responsibility. Remove the leading pipe from the definition and write it in front of the backtick reference.

guide.blueprintTitle: Create and use a basic macro
guide.verdictNote: The same reasoning explains why a macro can sit mid-pipeline with further commands after it. Nothing about a macro has to end a search.

docs.title: Search macro examples (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Definitions omit the leading pipe; the reference carries it.

questions.stem: A two-argument macro `foobar(2)` is defined with arguments `foo` and `bar`. Which invocations are equivalent according to the documentation's own example?

options.text: `` `foobar(1,2)` ``, `` `foobar(foo=1,bar=2)` `` and `` `foobar(bar=2,foo=1)` ``
options.explanation: The macros.conf example states these three forms are equivalent, so arguments can be positional or named, and named arguments can be reordered.

options.text: Only `` `foobar(1,2)` ``, because macro arguments are strictly positional
options.explanation: Named arguments are supported. This is the assumption the documentation's example specifically refutes.

options.text: Only the two named forms, because a two-argument macro requires named arguments
options.explanation: The positional form works and is the most common in practice.

options.text: None; a macro can take at most one argument
options.explanation: Macros routinely take several arguments; the count simply goes in the name.

questions.overallExplanation: Positional and named invocation both work, and named arguments may appear in any order. This is easy to miss because most examples in circulation only ever show the positional form.

questions.stem: What does `iseval = true` mean on a macro definition?

options.text: The definition is an eval expression returning a string, and that string becomes the macro's expansion.
options.explanation: The macro computes its own replacement text. The result is search text, not a field value.

options.text: The macro runs an eval command and adds a computed field to the results.
options.explanation: No field is created. The eval expression produces the text that replaces the macro reference.

options.text: The macro may only be used inside an eval expression.
options.explanation: There is no such placement restriction.

options.text: Argument validation is performed with eval syntax.
options.explanation: That is what the separate validation setting does.

questions.overallExplanation: iseval defaults to false. When set, the definition is evaluated as an eval expression and its returned string is substituted, which lets a macro build different search text depending on its arguments.

guide.blueprintTitle: Define arguments and variables for a macro
guide.verdictNote: Consistent with macros being textual: even an eval-backed macro produces text for the parser rather than data for the pipeline.

docs.title: macros.conf spec (Admin Manual 10.4)
docs.note: iseval: the definition is an eval expression returning a string representing the expansion.

questions.stem: A macro is created in Search and Reporting and shared at app level. A colleague working in a different app cannot use it. Why?

options.text: App-level sharing makes an object available only to users of that app; global use requires All apps.
options.explanation: The object is bound to the app context it was created in until it is promoted to All apps.

options.text: Macros cannot be shared between users under any circumstances.
options.explanation: They can be shared to an app or globally like other knowledge objects.

options.text: The colleague lacks the power role, which is required to invoke any macro.
options.explanation: Roles govern who can share and promote, not who can invoke a macro that is already visible to them.

options.text: Macros require a restart before other users can see them.
options.explanation: macros.conf is among the search-time files whose settings take effect without a restart.

questions.overallExplanation: Permission scope is the usual explanation for it works for me but not for them. Promote to All apps for cross-app use. No restart is needed either way.

guide.blueprintTitle: Create and use a basic macro
guide.verdictNote: The Admin Manual page on when a restart is required lists macros.conf among search-time files that take effect after an endpoint refresh.

docs.title: Manage knowledge object permissions (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: App-level sharing limits visibility to that app until promoted globally.

questions.stem: Which two statements about search macros are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: A macro definition can contain a full pipeline including multiple commands.
options.explanation: Because expansion is textual, anything valid as search text is valid in a definition.

options.text: A macro reference can be followed by further commands in the same search.
options.explanation: Nothing requires a macro to end a search. It substitutes text and the pipeline continues.

options.text: A macro with arguments must also define a validation expression and an error message.
options.explanation: Validation is optional. Arguments work without it.

options.text: Macros are configured under Settings, Fields alongside aliases and calculated fields.
options.explanation: Macros have their own page under Settings, Advanced search, Search macros.

questions.overallExplanation: A macro is text, so it composes freely: whole pipelines inside, more commands after. Validation is optional, and macros live under Advanced search rather than with the field-related objects.

guide.verdictNote: Knowing the Settings path matters: Settings, Advanced search, Search macros. Distractors routinely place them under Fields.
